conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I've been reviewing your case. You came in today with nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. Can you tell me more about what happened this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doc. I got up and suddenly the room started spinning. I’ve had this before, but it’s always scary. Then the nausea hit, and I vomited a few times. Right-side abdominal pain got worse too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. No fever or chills? Any chest pain when you vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever, but I did feel chills. And yeah, there’s a burning in my chest when I throw up, but not otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve given you ondansetron for nausea. Your labs show your liver enzymes are up, but about where they’ve been. No signs of infection so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, I hate throwing up. It makes me so weak. I’ve lost over ten pounds in a month. I can’t keep food down sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning. We’re going to look into why. We did a CT scan of your abdomen. It shows cirrhosis, which we expected, and some fecal loading in the colon. But nothing acute like a blockage or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fecal loading? You mean constipation? I’ve been a bit backed up, yeah.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And we’re wondering if your iron supplements might be making that worse. They can cause nausea and constipation, especially with liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take ferrous sulfate twice a day. Could that really be part of the problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be. We’re going to stop it for now and see if your symptoms improve. We don’t want to add anything that could irritate your stomach more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll stop it. But what about the dizziness and vomiting? Is it just from my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We also saw that your bicarbonate level is high, which suggests metabolic alkalosis. That can happen from repeated vomiting. We’ll monitor that and support you with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s all connected? Vomiting causing the imbalance?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And because you’re cirrhotic, your body handles fluids and electrolytes differently. We held your diuretics for now because you seemed a bit dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take furosemide and spironolactone. Should I keep skipping them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not long-term. We’ll restart them once you’re stable. But we may adjust the dose. Your spironolactone was 300 mg—quite high. We might reduce it to help with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it doesn’t cause fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. I haven’t vomited since yesterday afternoon. Nausea is still there but milder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re going to advance your diet to soft foods today. We also scheduled an upper endoscopy to check your stomach and duodenum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Endoscopy? I’ve had that before. Is it because of the ulcer they saw last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You have a known duodenal polyp with an ulcer on it. We want to see if it’s changed and if it might be contributing to your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they biopsy it this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They may not. Given your low platelets and cirrhosis, there’s a higher risk of bleeding. But they’ll assess it carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I just hope it’s not getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll know more after the procedure. We also ordered a gastric emptying study to check for gastroparesis, since delayed emptying can cause nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that test last time. They said it was normal, but I still feel full fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it can be borderline. We’ll compare the results. In the meantime, keep sipping fluids and let us know if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, your endoscopy was done yesterday. The duodenal ulcer is still there—about 2 cm, friable, but not bleeding. They didn’t biopsy it due to bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Friable? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means the tissue is easily irritated or bleeds. It’s consistent with chronic duodenitis, which you’ve had for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not cancerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. It’s a benign polyp, but we’ll monitor it. The good news is no active bleeding or new ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the gastric emptying test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It showed moderately delayed emptying. Twenty percent of food was still in your stomach after four hours—normal is under ten percent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I do have gastroparesis? But I’m not diabetic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cirrhosis can cause it too. Slowed motility, portal hypertension. We’ll manage it with diet and medications like ondansetron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to small meals. Any other tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your H. pylori blood test came back negative. So that’s not contributing. Your liver function is stable, and your alkalosis is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Mr. Johnson. You’ve done well. No vomiting in two days, eating solids, labs are better. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting furosemide at 60 mg daily. Spironolactone will be reduced to 200 mg. And continue pantoprazole, lactulose, rifaximin, and nadolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no more iron?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’ll reassess later. If you need iron, we might consider IV, but not now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the duodenal ulcer? Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable. We’ll follow up with GI. They may want a repeat endoscopy in a few months when your platelets are higher.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re cleared to go home. Keep taking your meds as discussed. Watch for vomiting, severe pain, or black stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll follow up with hepatology and GI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re still on the transplant list, so keep all appointments. Eat small, frequent meals, stay hydrated, and avoid alcohol completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not drinking, doc. I know what’s at stake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll send all results to your team. If nausea returns, call your doctor or come in. Otherwise, take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Patel. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. We’ll see you in follow-up. Safe trip home.
